entries.topicDescription: Managing object creation and dependencies with Hilt, Koin, and manual DI patterns.

tips.title: Constructor injection over field injection keeps dependencies explicit and testable
tips.content:
Field-injected dependencies (a @Inject-annotated var, or a service
locator lookup inside a class) hide what a class actually needs from
anyone reading its public API — you have to inspect the implementation
to know what to provide in a test.

Constructor injection makes every dependency visible in the class's
signature, so a unit test can construct the class directly with fakes or
mocks with no DI framework involved at all — Hilt and Koin both support
constructor injection as the preferred pattern for exactly this
testability benefit.

tips.title: Use @Binds for interface implementations and @Provides for everything else
tips.content:
In Hilt, @Binds tells the container which implementation to use for an interface. It is an abstract function with no body, so it generates less code than a @Provides function. Use @Provides when you must call code to create the object: a third-party class you can't annotate, or one that needs a builder such as Retrofit or Room.

Both live in a @Module annotated with @InstallIn to choose the component (and so the scope) they are available in.

tips.title: Scopes decide how long an injected object lives
tips.content:
An unscoped binding creates a new instance every time it is injected. Adding a scope annotation makes Hilt reuse one instance for the lifetime of the matching component: @Singleton for the whole app, @ActivityRetainedScoped across configuration changes, @ViewModelScoped for one ViewModel, and @ActivityScoped for one Activity.

Scope only what genuinely needs to be shared or is expensive to build. A scope that is wider than necessary keeps objects (and anything they reference) alive longer than needed.

tips.title: Swap real dependencies for fakes in tests with @TestInstallIn
tips.content:
Constructor injection lets a plain unit test pass fakes directly. For instrumented or Hilt-based UI tests, Hilt can replace a production module with a test module: annotate the test module with @TestInstallIn, naming the module it replaces, and every injection point receives the fake.

Combine it with @HiltAndroidTest and a HiltAndroidRule so the test gets its own component. Fakes keep such tests fast and deterministic instead of hitting the real network.

tips.title: Compile-time DI (Hilt) versus runtime DI (Koin): where errors show up
tips.content:
Hilt (built on Dagger) validates the dependency graph at compile time, so a missing binding fails the build. Koin resolves dependencies at runtime, which keeps setup lightweight and works across Kotlin Multiplatform, but a missing definition only fails when that dependency is first requested.

With Koin, catch that class of error early by verifying your modules in a test, so a forgotten definition breaks CI rather than a user's screen.
